text:
Defense Health officials are advising Tricare beneficiaries that the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System, or DEERS, will be temporarily unavailable this weekend.

The planned outage is scheduled to begin at 9 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Friday, Oct. 9, and end Sunday, Oct. 11. As of Thursday, information was not available about what specific time the outage is expected to end on Sunday.

During the outage, beneficiaries won’t be able to make any updates to their DEERS record. Pharmacies and healthcare providers may not be able to check a patient’s Tricare eligibility.

Officials note that there are other benefits systems that rely on DEERS, and the outage may affect those systems, too.

The Defense Manpower Data Center is updating DEERS, and it will be moving to a new cloud environment.

“The Defense Health Agency is working closely with DMDC during this time,” officials said in an announcement about the planned outage. “The goal is to keep any disruption as small as possible.”

DEERS is a database of information about military personnel, Defense Department and military service civilians and their family members. To get Tricare coverage, beneficiaries must be registered in DEERS.

Beneficiaries who need to make changes, or who need to check their information in DEERS, should do so before the weekend by visiting milconnect before 9 p.m. Friday.

This year’s Tricare Open Season begins Nov. 9 and ends Dec. 8. During that time, beneficiaries can enroll in or change their health plan for the next year. Changes made during open season will take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

text:
A change to the login system for the MHS Genesis medical records’ patient portal has caused headaches for military health beneficiaries, as many have found they can’t access their entire family’s accounts.

The Defense Health Agency announced in mid-September that it was switching from the older login process, DS Logon, to a new program called myAuth for the MHS Genesis system.

DS Logon required lengthy passwords that had to be changed frequently, while myAuth promised a more “user-friendly experience” and improved security, according to DHA.

Following the transition, however, some patients have been unable to access their own medical records. Sponsors must grant access permission to their spouses and dependents, and in some cases, dependent children aren’t showing up on either parent’s accounts.

“Just stop changing things. Every time one system finally starts working and everyone gets used to it, you switch it up. Tricare online was fine. Genesis was fine,” an Army spouse wrote on Tricare’s Facebook page.

In response, DHA announced Sept. 25 that the patient portal would remain “fully accessible via DS Logon.”

But beneficiaries say when they use the old DS Logon system, they are redirected to the myAuth login page and still cannot access family records.

“I can log in and see all my stuff. I can send out messages and receive them … but nothing for my kids,” a military spouse said in a direct message to Military Times. “To message their doctor, I have to send a message through my name and put in the subject my child’s name.”

DHA spokeswoman Brenda Campbell said Thursday that DHA is working with the Defense Manpower Data Center to resolve the issues. DMDC manages the myAuth system and is responsible for the transition from DS Logon, she said.

“MyAuth is a new digital login that replaces DS Logon for accessing [Defense Department] websites and applications, like the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal. We are aware of the issues associated with the transition and are providing that feedback to DMDC to ensure appropriate fixes are applied,” Campbell said.

According to DHA, MyAuth will provide more ways to log in to the MHS Patient Portal, allow for use of a Common Access Card, verification through the Okta mobile app and other authentication choices.

It also has a simpler interface that is more user-friendly, DHA officials added.

“The switch to myAuth means a simpler, more secure experience in MHS Genesis Patient Portal,” they said.

Another change to the Defense Department’s information technology systems will affect Military Health System patients and Tricare beneficiaries this weekend: a planned outage of the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System, or DEERS, as it transitions to a cloud-based system.

DEERS will be offline from 9 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Friday, Oct. 9, to Sunday, Oct. 11, although the Pentagon has not specified a time.

During the outage, beneficiaries won’t be able to update their DEERS records and pharmacies and healthcare providers may not be able to check a patient’s Tricare eligibility.

The DEERS database contains information about military personnel, retirees, family members and civilian employees.

text:
An Oklahoma chiropractor and business owner has been sentenced to 14 years in federal prison for his role in a years-long scheme that tried to defraud Medicare, TRICARE and the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs out of more than $30 million.

“Yesterday's 14-year sentence shows that health care fraud does not pay,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Department of Justice's National Fraud Enforcement Division. “The Department is committed to bringing to justice those who corrupt our health care system by paying illegal kickbacks, submitting false claims, deceiving programs that serve our seniors, service members, and veterans, and treating sensitive patient information like a commodity to be bought and sold.”

Authorities said Dr. Mark Loftis paid more than $1 million in illegal kickbacks, including through a shell marketing company, to marketers, purported telemedicine companies and a call center. Investigators said the call center persuaded elderly and disabled Americans to disclose personal information and receive medical equipment they did not need.

Prosecutors also said Loftis and co-conspirators purchased sham doctors’ orders for orthotic braces, continuous glucose monitors and other medical equipment that were generated by telemedicine doctors and nurse practitioners who never examined or spoke to the beneficiaries.

“Healthcare fraud drains millions of dollars from federally funded programs, and we all pay the price,” said Special Agent in Charge Rodney Crawford of the FBI Tampa Field Office. “Today’s sentence underscores the FBI’s steadfast commitment to aggressively pursuing those who engage in kickback schemes and other fraudulent practices.”

The DOJ said the group submitted more than $30 million in false and fraudulent claims and was paid more than $8 million. In one example cited by prosecutors, the group billed for eight braces for a single beneficiary.

“Fraud against federal health care programs is a direct attack on the public’s trust and on the vulnerable individuals these programs are meant to protect, and the jury’s verdict and sentencing of Mark Loftis demonstrate that schemes of this kind will be met with decisive action and significant consequences,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L. Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General.

After a 12-day jury trial, Loftis was convicted of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud.

In addition to the prison sentence, he was ordered to pay more than $8 million in restitution and to forfeit more than $560,000.

text:
An Oklahoma business owner and chiropractor was sentenced yesterday to 14 years in prison for his role in a years-long scheme that attempted to bilk Medicare, TRICARE, and the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA) out of over $30 million for orthotics braces, continuous glucose monitors, and other durable medical equipment (DME) that beneficiaries did not want or need.

“Yesterday's 14-year sentence shows that health care fraud does not pay,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Department of Justice's National Fraud Enforcement Division. “The Department is committed to bringing to justice those who corrupt our health care system by paying illegal kickbacks, submitting false claims, deceiving programs that serve our seniors, service members, and veterans, and treating sensitive patient information like a commodity to be bought and sold.”

“Fraud against federal health care programs is a direct attack on the public’s trust and on the vulnerable individuals these programs are meant to protect, and the jury’s verdict and sentencing of Mark Loftis demonstrate that schemes of this kind will be met with decisive action and significant consequences,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L. Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General. “HHS-OIG will not hesitate to investigate and dismantle criminal conduct wherever it threatens the integrity of federal programs, and this case reflects the unwavering commitment of our agency and our law-enforcement partners to safeguard taxpayer dollars and ensure that those who defraud the government are held fully accountable.”

“Healthcare fraud drains millions of dollars from federally funded programs, and we all pay the price,” said Special Agent in Charge Rodney Crawford of the FBI Tampa Field Office. “Today’s sentence underscores the FBI’s steadfast commitment to aggressively pursuing those who engage in kickback schemes and other fraudulent practices.”

“As the law enforcement arm of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General, the Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS) is committed to safeguarding the integrity of the TRICARE program,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Nakia M. Alexander of the DCIS Southeast Field Office. “This investigation is an example of a healthcare fraud scheme that directly affected American service members and their families. I applaud the collaborative work of the investigative agencies and the Department of Justice that led to today’s sentencing.”

“Fraud schemes targeting VA programs and services compromise their integrity and divert funds from veterans who rely on these benefits,” said Inspector General Cheryl L. Mason, Department of Veterans Affairs. “The VA OIG works every day with our law enforcement partners to identify fraudsters and hold them accountable.”

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Dr. Mark Loftis, 39, of Cushing, Oklahoma, and his co-conspirators did not disclose to Medicare the ownership and management of the DME company Back Pain Home Supplies LLC dba EZ Medical Supply. Loftis and his co-conspirators hid from Medicare that unenrolled entities were billing claims through the DME company. Lofits paid over a million dollars in illegal kickbacks, including through a shell marketing company, to marketers, purported telemedicine companies, and a call center that persuaded elderly and disabled Americans to disclose their personal information and receive DME they did not need. Loftis and his co-conspirators also purchased sham doctors’ orders for orthotic braces, continuous glucose monitors, and DME that were generated by telemedicine doctors and nurse practitioners who never examined, and often never spoke to, the beneficiaries. Loftis and his co-conspirators submitted over $30 million in false and fraudulent claims and were paid over $8 million. Loftis and his co-conspirators frequently billed for multiple orthotic braces at a time, including in one example eight braces for a single beneficiary.

After a 12-day jury trial ending in July 2026, Loftis was convicted of conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud. In addition to the prison sentence, Loftis was ordered to pay over $8 million in restitution and to forfeit over $560,000.

HHS-OIG, FBI, DCIS, and VA-OIG investigated the case.

Assistant Deputy Chief Catherine Wagner and Trial Attorney Raymond Beckering III of the National Fraud Enforcement Division’s Health Care Fraud Section prosecuted the case.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

text:
In October 2016, the Pentagon’s health system, TRICARE, scrapped its caps on mental health visits and inpatient days, cut outpatient copays from $25 to $12 for some beneficiaries, expanded coverage for addiction treatment, and loosened the paperwork that kept civilian therapists out of its network. TRICARE is the insurer of record for 9.5 million service members, retirees, and their families

Nearly a decade later, Jangho Yoon of the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences in Bethesda has published the first system-wide test asking if that reform has changed the outcome that mattered most: whether fewer military beneficiaries have attempted suicide.

Writing in Health Economics Review, Yoon draws on more than 140 million person-quarters of claims data from the Military Health System Data Repository, covering 2.3 million active-duty troops, 1.5 million retirees under 65, and 5.7 million dependents between early 2015 and early 2020.

Because every beneficiary received the reform at once, there was no untreated group to compare against. Yoon instead uses an interrupted time-series design that looked for a break in the trend when parity took effect, with individual fixed effects to absorb differences in sex, race, and service branch.

The headline finding was that parity worked — but unevenly. All three groups saw an immediate drop in medically attended suicide attempts: roughly five fewer per 100,000 among active-duty service members, four fewer among retirees, and seven fewer among dependents, or declines of 11, 20, and 16% against the pre-reform baseline. The divergence came afterward.

Retirees kept improving by about 1.6 attempts per 100,000 each quarter, and dependents by 3.1. Over the 14 quarters Yoon tracked, the cumulative reductions reached 241 fewer attempts per 100,000 retirees and 435 fewer per 100,000 dependents, which the paper translates into roughly 3,600 fewer attempts among retirees and some 23,000 fewer among family members.

Active-duty troops tell a different story. Their initial dip did not hold. The quarter-by-quarter estimates hovered around zero, the cumulative effect lost statistical significance after about 21 months, and the post-reform slope was flat.

Junior enlisted personnel, the group under the heaviest occupational stress, showed the largest immediate decline and then a statistically significant reversal, a pattern Yoon reads as parity encouraging help-seeking only for the gains to be eroded by career pressures and stigma.

Yoon’s explanation turned on how the reform touched each group. Retirees and dependents paid copays and often relied on civilian providers, so cheaper care and a bigger network relaxed both financial and practical barriers at once. Active-duty members already paid nothing and got most of their care at military treatment facilities, so the reform reached them only through the supply side, and only partly.

Two-thirds of active-duty troops lived in areas designated as psychiatrist shortage zones, and 6% of all beneficiaries lived where there was no psychiatrist at all. What the reform could not touch were the barriers particular to military life: fears about confidentiality, career repercussions, and the cost of being seen to seek help inside a close-knit institution. For that population, Yoon concludes, parity should be seen as “a necessary but insufficient strategy for suicide prevention.”

The paper has arrived amid worsening trends. Suicide deaths among active-duty troops rose from 24.3 per 100,000 in 2021 to 28.2 in 2023, and the raw attempt rate in Yoon’s data climbed throughout the study period regardless of parity, peaking at about 73 per 100,000 in early 2019.

Diagnoses of anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder nearly doubled among service members between 2019 and 2023, and mental disorders accounted for the largest share of inpatient bed days in the force that year.

The Pentagon’s own annual report on military suicide for 2023 called the long-term rise statistically significant and conceded that “it is not possible to identify a single root cause that might explain this trend.”

Yoon acknowledges these limits. Claims captured only attempts that reached a clinic or emergency room. The reform changed several things at once, so the study cannot say which lever mattered. Guard and Reserve members were excluded, and without a control group, concurrent events cannot be fully ruled out, though the results held up under alternative time trends, a logit model, and a trimming procedure for the linear probability model.

The study points to the Brandon Act, signed in late 2021 to give service members confidential access to mental health care, as the kind of cultural reform that might eventually let parity do for troops what it already did for their families.

text:
SAN FRANCISCO — Older veterans who sustain a traumatic brain injury (TBI) are significantly more likely than their peers to have been diagnosed with neurologic conditions such as dementia, Parkinson’s disease, stroke or epilepsy even before the injury occurs, according to a new retrospective cohort study. The findings suggest that these conditions might not only develop after TBI but also contribute to circumstances that increase the risk of sustaining one.

The study, published in Neurology, examined electronic health records from the VA and found a bidirectional relationship between TBI and several neurologic disorders. Researchers say the findings highlight the importance of recognizing fall risk much earlier in patients with neurologic disease.

“We’ve known from previous studies that traumatic brain injury increases the risk of conditions such as dementia and Parkinson’s disease later in life,” said Carrie B. Peltz, PhD, a researcher with NCIRE (the Veterans Health Research Institute) and an affiliate at UCSF, where she studies traumatic brain injury, dementia and Alzheimer’s disease risk factors in veterans. “What has been studied much less is what may be happening before the traumatic brain injury.”

Peltz said much of the previous research on TBI has focused on younger adults or on the immediate consequences of injury. Her research group has instead concentrated on older adults and the longer-term effects of TBI. While earlier studies demonstrated that TBI increases the risk of neurologic disorders, few had examined whether some of those same conditions might already be present before the injury and contribute to falls that ultimately result in TBI.

The investigators identified 13,801 veterans age 55 years and older who experienced an acute TBI and matched them with more than 41,000 veterans without TBI. The average age of participants was nearly 78 years.1

Compared with veterans who did not experience TBI, those who later sustained a traumatic brain injury had markedly higher rates of several neurologic disorders during the year preceding the injury, the study found. The incidence of stroke, dementia and Parkinson’s disease was approximately three times higher, while epilepsy occurred more than four times as often. The associations remained significant even after researchers adjusted for medical comorbidities and healthcare utilization.

The elevated risk did not end with the injury. During the year following TBI, veterans experienced significantly higher rates of stroke, epilepsy and dementia than they had before the injury, supporting previous evidence that traumatic brain injury can accelerate neurologic decline.

Peltz said the findings likely reflect the ways neurologic disorders affect mobility, balance, coordination and judgment, making falls—and the resulting head injuries—more likely.

“Parkinson’s disease is probably the one most people think about,” she said, noting that impaired motor control increases fall risk. However, stroke, dementia and epilepsy also can contribute. Patients with dementia, for example, might forget that they need assistance when walking or fail to remember to use a walker, while stroke survivors may have weakness or impaired coordination that increases the likelihood of falling.

Because falls are a leading cause of TBI in older adults, the researchers believe clinicians should consider implementing fall-prevention strategies much earlier in the course of neurologic disease.

“I think emphasizing fall prevention earlier in the disease process is important,” Peltz told U.S. Medicine. “There are a lot of tools available, including physical therapy, occupational therapy and home safety evaluations that can help people move more safely and reduce their risk.”

She noted that clinicians often begin addressing fall prevention only after patients develop more obvious motor symptoms. However, earlier intervention may help prevent traumatic brain injuries before they occur. Physical and occupational therapy, balance training, evaluation of assistive devices and simple home modifications such as removing tripping hazards and improving household safety can all reduce fall risk for vulnerable patients.

“The rates were three to four times higher in people who went on to have a traumatic brain injury,” she said. “I think it’s a little more significant than people may realize.”

Preventing TBI could have benefits beyond avoiding the immediate injury itself, Peltz said. “Traumatic brain injury sets off a whole cascade. Preventing those injuries may help prevent future neurologic problems and keep existing conditions from becoming worse.”

The researchers also considered whether TBI might simply bring previously undiagnosed neurologic disease to medical attention because patients receive more extensive evaluations after a head injury. To reduce that possibility, they excluded neurologic diagnoses made within approximately two weeks of the TBI when comparing conditions occurring before and after the injury.

Although the study included only older veterans, the findings reinforce the importance of recognizing fall risk in patients with neurologic disorders and suggest that earlier preventive interventions may reduce traumatic brain injuries and their long-term consequences.

Peltz and her colleagues noted that additional studies are needed to determine whether similar associations exist in non-veteran populations and whether earlier fall-prevention efforts can reduce both TBI and subsequent neurologic complications.

text:
NEWARK, N.J. – A Massachusetts doctor was sentenced for her role in telemedicine health care fraud and kickback schemes that resulted in more than $40 million in fraudulent claims to Medicare and TRICARE, U.S. Attorney Robert Frazer announced.

Le Thu, 71, of Boston, Massachusetts, pleaded guilty before U.S. District Judge Susan D. Wigenton in Newark, in May 2025, to one count of an indictment, charging her with conspiracy to violate the Federal Anti-Kickback statute and, in June 2025, to a two-count information, charging her with false statements related to health care matters. Thu was sentenced on October 6, 2026, on all counts to 36 months’ imprisonment with two years’ supervised release, and ordered to pay over $27 million in restitution.

According to documents filed in this case and statements made in court:

From May 2014 through April 2017, Thu participated in a conspiracy in which she received kickbacks from a telemedicine company in exchange for approving hundreds of prescriptions for durable medical equipment and compounded medications. Thu agreed to accept kickback payments of approximately $35 from the telemedicine company in exchange for each prescription she approved, knowing that certain of the prescriptions would be used to bill TRICARE, a health care program of the U.S. Department of Defense. TRICARE paid pharmacies hundreds of thousands of dollars for compounded medications that were procured through kickbacks Thu received.

From March 2017 through November 2020, Thu participated in a second telemedicine health care fraud scheme in connection with payments for genetic tests and durable medical equipment for Medicare beneficiaries. On behalf of multiple telemedicine companies, Thu signed, and caused others who had no medical training to sign, false medical documentation and orders for genetic tests and durable medical equipment. The documentation made it appear that Thu had exercised her medical judgment in approving the orders and, in certain instances, that she would use the genetic test results to treat beneficiaries. Thu, however, had not interacted with or provided any medical care to the beneficiaries prior to signing, or having others sign, the doctors’ orders. Thu signed thousands of such orders that contained statements she knew were false and material to Medicare in exchange for payments to her totaling more than $200,000. As a result, Thu caused durable medical equipment suppliers and laboratories to submit more than $40 million in claims to Medicare based on doctors’ orders containing materially false representations, for which Medicare paid more than $27 million.

text:
What providers should know about DOJ’s enforcement focus on wound care and skin substitutes

The Department of Justice (DOJ) and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) have made wound care services and skin substitute product manufacturers some of their primary healthcare fraud enforcement targets. The recent string of False Claims Act (FCA) settlements makes clear that scrutiny of these providers shows no signs of slowing.

In December 2025, DOJ announced resolution of the largest wound graft enforcement matter to date, resolved through criminal pleas and an FCA settlement, based on theories of medical necessity and inappropriate billing. The owners of several Arizona wound graft companies, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud and wire fraud, were each sentenced to over 14 years in prison for orchestrating a scheme that generated over $1.2 billion in false claims for medically unnecessary wound grafts submitted to Medicare, TRICARE, and CHAMPVA between 2022 and 2024. The owners and their marketing company separately agreed to pay $309 million to resolve FCA liability. Sales representatives with no medical training allegedly identified elderly and hospice patients with wounds of any kind, then directed nurse practitioners to apply the largest, most expensive skin substitutes—regardless of medical necessity. One of the wound graft company owners allegedly received over $279 million in kickbacks from the graft distributor in exchange for steering business its way.

Smaller wound care providers are also not flying under the radar. In July 2025, a Florida dermatology practice and affiliated surgery center agreed to pay $847,394 to resolve allegations of upcoding wound repair claims following skin cancer surgery. DOJ alleged that over a seven-year period from 2017 to 2024, the practices billed simple linear repairs as if they were more complex flap repairs, and smaller flap repairs as if they were larger—with both practices triggering higher Medicare reimbursement. Brought under the FCA, the relator took home over $150,000 of the recovery—a reminder that former employees remain one of DOJ’s most effective sources for uncovering coding-level fraud that might otherwise go undetected even in the era of DOJ’s increased data-driven enforcement.

Not every FCA wound care enforcement theory turns on medical necessity or provider coding accuracy alone. In November 2025, DOJ announced a $45 million settlement with one of the nation’s largest providers of specialty wound care to nursing home and skilled nursing facility residents. In addition to allegations of medically unnecessary debridement procedures and improper coding, DOJ focused heavily on the company’s billing system itself. The government alleged the company had manipulated its electronic health record (EHR) and billing software to default to the higher-reimbursed billing code, regardless of the procedure actually performed. Under the five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement signed with the Department of Health and Human Services – Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG), the company must implement a compliance program, conduct risk assessments, and hire an Independent Review Organization to review its claims and health information technology systems.

Most recently, on September 2, 2026, a Kentucky-based provider of at-home wound care services agreed to pay $2,646,186.72 to resolve allegations that it violated the FCA by overbilling Medicare and TRICARE for costly skin substitute products. The settlement is part of a broader investigative initiative known as “Operation Skin Scam,” built specifically to uncover fraud schemes involving expensive skin substitute materials. The allegations here turned not on medical necessity or upcoding, but on the invoice itself: DOJ claimed the provider billed Medicare and TRICARE using inflated purchase prices for the products, thus inflating the reimbursement. This Operation’s name leaves little doubt: DOJ will continue to aggressively pursue fraudulent skin substitute billing across the industry.

Where providers should focus risk assessment and enforcement efforts

These four matters make clear that wound care is now a top-tier enforcement priority for DOJ, HHS-OIG, and CMS alike. Wound care providers and companies that manufacture, distribute, or bill for skin substitutes should expect continued, coordinated scrutiny. Providers should treat this as a priority compliance area. Proactive auditing and compliance monitoring in the following areas, in particular, remain essential to mitigate risk in this era of heightened scrutiny: (1) medical necessity, (2) debridement coding, (3) skin substitute billing and acquisition cost, (4) documentation, which should accurately reflect the patient’s condition and the care provided, (5) EHR default settings and billing controls, and (6) financial incentives and vendor and distributor relationships.

RENO, Nev. — Michigan Democrat Sen. Elissa Slotkin brought her national profile to Northern Nevada this week, headlining a Washoe County Democrat fundraiser where congressional candidate Teresa Benitez-Thompson was among the featured guests.

Slotkin delivered the keynote address Wednesday at the Washoe County Democrat Party’s “Power the Blue Wave” dinner at the Grand Sierra Resort in Reno. The party advertised Benitez-Thompson, the Democrat nominee for Nevada’s 2nd Congressional District, as a special guest alongside other statewide Democrat candidates.

Slotkin’s Nevada swing comes as Benitez-Thompson receives increasing national attention. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added her to its “Red to Blue” program this week, signaling that national Democrats are investing resources in her bid for the Republican-held seat.

But Slotkin also arrives in Nevada carrying a congressional record that could sharpen one of the culture-war divides already surrounding Benitez-Thompson.

“I’ve always fought for equality and LGBTQ+ rights, including again yesterday by voting last night to protect access to gender-affirming care for military families,” Slotkin said in July 2023.

The underlying vote involved an amendment to the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act sponsored by Republican Rep. Ralph Norman of South Carolina. The amendment prohibited gender-transition procedures, including surgery or medication, for minor dependents enrolled in the military’s Exceptional Family Member Program. It passed the House 222-210. Slotkin voted against it.

Slotkin also opposed a separate amendment that prohibited TRICARE and the Department of Defense from covering sex-reassignment surgeries and gender hormone treatments for transgender individuals. That amendment passed 222-211.

Supporters of those restrictions argued taxpayers should not be responsible for financing gender-transition procedures through military health programs. Opponents, including Slotkin, argued that military families should retain access to medical care and that parents and doctors should be able to make those decisions.

The issue has particular relevance for Benitez-Thompson because her own Nevada legislative record has already become part of the campaign.

In 2015, Benitez-Thompson spoke against Assembly Bill 375, legislation that would have required students to use school bathrooms, locker rooms and showers designated for their biological sex while requiring schools to provide alternative accommodations for transgender students.

“Regulating bathroom use?” Benitez-Thompson told lawmakers. “Such regulation is the exact opposite of efficient government, meaningful government, good public policy.” She voted against the measure, which ultimately failed 22-20.

Slotkin’s appearance alongside Benitez-Thompson therefore brings more than national fundraising muscle to Reno. It also puts renewed attention on two Democrats whose records show opposition to government restrictions on transgender-related policies, one in Congress involving military health care and the other in Carson City involving public-school facilities.

Axios reported Slotkin’s Nevada trip is also drawing attention because she is widely viewed as a possible 2028 presidential contender, with Nevada positioned near the front of the Democrat presidential nominating calendar.

During the outage, beneficiaries won't be able to make any updates to their DEERS record.
Pharmacies and healthcare providers may not be able to check a patient's Tricare eligibility.
Officials note that there are other benefits systems that rely on DEERS, and the outage may affect those systems, too.

text:
Defense Health officials are advising Tricare beneficiaries that the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System, or DEERS, will be temporarily unavailable this weekend.

The planned outage is scheduled to begin at 9 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Friday, Oct. 9, and end Sunday, Oct. 11. As of Thursday, information was not available about what specific time the outage is expected to end on Sunday.

During the outage, beneficiaries won't be able to make any updates to their DEERS record. Pharmacies and healthcare providers may not be able to check a patient's Tricare eligibility.

Officials note that there are other benefits systems that rely on DEERS, and the outage may affect those systems, too.

The Defense Manpower Data Center is updating DEERS, and it will be moving to a new cloud environment.

"The Defense Health Agency is working closely with DMDC during this time," officials said in an announcement about the planned outage. "The goal is to keep any disruption as small as possible."

DEERS is a database of information about military personnel, Defense Department and military service civilians and their family members. To get Tricare coverage, beneficiaries must be registered in DEERS.

Beneficiaries who need to make changes, or who need to check their information in DEERS, should do so before the weekend by visiting milconnect before 9 p.m. Friday.

This year's Tricare Open Season begins Nov. 9 and ends Dec. 8. During that time, beneficiaries can enroll in or change their health plan for the next year. Changes made during open season will take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

title: Bill stalled in Congress would expand IVF access for active-duty military families
description:
Arwen and Chad Anderson said they always wanted to start a family after getting married in 2019.
Dr. Angeline Beltsos, a reproductive endocrinologist with Brown Fertility in Tampa, said IVF coverage should be available more broadly.
Beltsos said her husband also served in the Navy and that IVF coverage options were not available at that time.
“Their biological clock is ticking, but they may not have the opportunity to try when they are active military,” Beltsos said.
“We were going to come up with the money because this is one of the most important things in our life,” Chad Anderson said.
text:
TAMPA, Fla. — A bill stalled in Congress would expand access to in vitro fertilization and other fertility-related care for active-duty military members and their dependents, including families in Florida with limited options under TRICARE.

Arwen and Chad Anderson said they always wanted to start a family after getting married in 2019. For the past five years, they have tried to conceive through IVF.

“We've had three full cycles. So it kind of gets repetitive, kind of blends together,” Chad Anderson said.

The couple said they are preparing to start another cycle despite previous disappointment.

“When people hear IVF, and I was one of them, you automatically think you're going to have a baby,” Arwen Anderson said. “But sometimes, it just, for some of us, it doesn't work out like that.”

Chad Anderson served in the Navy for 10 years before ending his service in 2021. He said their IVF journey began after his military service, but he tried to learn more about his fertility while still serving.

“I did try to get testing while I wasn't married, just to see if I was fertile or not, and they would not do anything like that,” Chad Anderson said.

The IVF for Military Families Act would require the "Secretary of Defense to ensure fertility-related care for active-duty uniformed service members and their dependents is covered under TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select." The legislation was originally introduced in 2025.

TRICARE’s website says assisted reproductive technology services, including IVF, are not covered. There are exceptions, including some military hospitals that offer assisted reproductive technology services through reproductive endocrinology and infertility clinics, but none are in Florida.

Dr. Angeline Beltsos, a reproductive endocrinologist with Brown Fertility in Tampa, said IVF coverage should be available more broadly.

“Infertility can affect anyone, and for those that are serving in the military, that may have to delay getting tested or their treatment is a shame when we could be helping them,” Beltsos said.

Beltsos said her husband also served in the Navy and that IVF coverage options were not available at that time. She said active military patients today often have to explore other coverage options.

“Their biological clock is ticking, but they may not have the opportunity to try when they are active military,” Beltsos said.

Chad Anderson said he has explored returning to the Navy reserves for TRICARE coverage, but he and Arwen Anderson said the time apart would not be worth it.

“We were going to come up with the money because this is one of the most important things in our life,” Chad Anderson said. “So we would take a loan if we needed to or find a way.”

text:
By Douglas Holl, Defense Health Agency-Public Health As the military community observes Domestic Violence Prevention Month this October 2026, experts at Defense Health Agency-Public Health are urging service members, military leaders, and families to look beyond physical violence and recognize the broader, nonphysical "spectrum of abuse" that can undermine unit and family readiness.

The campaign arrives alongside the release of the Department of War’s Report on Child Abuse and Neglect and Domestic Abuse in the Military for Fiscal Year 2024, which documented 8,076 domestic abuse incidents across the military branches that met official clinical criteria. Of those verified incidents, physical abuse accounted for 68.2% of cases, while emotional or psychological abuse made up 25.6%. These statistics underscore the critical reality that domestic abuse often occurs without a single physical mark.

"When I use the phrase 'spectrum of abuse,' I want service members to understand that abuse can go beyond a black eye or other physical form of abuse," said Army Maj. Michelle Worsley, licensed clinical social worker and deputy director of the Health Promotion and Wellness directorate at DHA-PH in Aberdeen, Maryland. "Domestic violence rarely exists by itself. While physical abuse may be the behavior most people recognize, abusive behaviors can occur before, alongside, or without physical violence."

According to Worsley, domestic abuse involves patterns of behavior used to establish power, control, or intimidation, including limiting financial access, stalking, digital tracking, degradation, and isolating a partner from support networks.

Operational stress versusabuse

The high-tempo nature of military life, including frequent Permanent Change of Station moves, intense training cycles, and deployments, places unique stressors on relationships. However, clinical experts emphasize that operational stress must never be used to justify controlling behavior.

"I emphasize that military life creates stress,” said Worsley. “Stress is normal. Abuse is not. Normal conflict can be uncomfortable at times, but within it, both partners retain their voice. They can disagree, cool down, revisit the issue, compromise, and continue to make independent choices without fearing retaliation."

When relationships cross the line into abuse, a partner's stress increasingly becomes a justification for control.

"A PCS doesn’t justify taking away their spouse’s access to money," said Worsley. "A deployment doesn’t justify monitoring every communication their spouse has. And a hard day at work or home doesn’t justify threatening or humiliating their spouse."

Navigating the reporting pathways

For active duty service members or beneficiaries seeking help, the DOW offers two distinct paths through the Family Advocacy Program, both of which grant full access to medical care, victim advocacy, and professional safety planning:

"Choosing a restricted report does not mean choosing to go without care," said Worsley. "With both restricted and unrestricted reports, victims can still receive medical care and treatment, confidential counseling, crisis intervention, support services, safety planning, and risk assessment."

Importantly, Worsley noted that restricted reporting is only available to adult victims. There is no option for restricted reporting in any cases involving child abuse.

Actionable steps for peer support and leadership

Peer-to-peer and leadership support are the first lines of defense in the barracks and motor pools. For single service members concerned about a "battle buddy," Worsley advised starting a private, judgment-free conversation. Asking a simple question like,"I've noticed you haven't seemed like yourself lately. Are you okay?"can establish a lifeline.

For small-unit leaders, the priority must shift from clinical diagnosis to immediate safety, connection, and normalizing help-seeking behavior.

"Small-unit leaders can play a more active role in reducing the stigma associated with seeking domestic abuse or relationship counseling by normalizing preventive help seeking," said Worsley. "Don’t just introduce or talk about FAP when an incident occurs. Talk about relationship education and resources available alongside the discussions we routinely have pertaining to maintaining overall unit readiness."

DOW and national support resources

If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic abuse, confidential help is available 24/7. You do not have to navigate this alone:

Military Leaders Healthy Connections Toolkit (Military OneSource)

National Domestic Violence Hotline:Call 1-800-799-SAFE (7233) or text "START" to 88788 for free, confidential support.

**Call 1-800-342-9647 or visitMilitary OneSource**to access the Domestic Abuse Victim Advocate locator and connect with local installation FAP resources.

text:
Federal retirees in one online forum are grappling with an increasingly difficult question: When Federal Employees Health Benefits premiums climb into five figures, is it still worth staying put?

For some families looking ahead to 2027, Blue Cross Blue Shield coverage alone could exceed $10,000 per year.

Here's what to know

The conversation began in a Reddit thread on r/FedRetirees where the OP laid out the projected cost of staying with Blue Cross Blue Shield: "With the latest increase, for 2027 it will be $10k+ a year for BCBS Basic for a family. BCBS Standard is close to $13K." They then asked the question driving the discussion: "Is going ACA and managing income carefully to max out subsidies the better play now?"

One retiree responded with their own numbers. They said they currently insure themselves and their husband through BCBS Standard for $890 a month, but plan to remove him from the policy when he turns 65 so he can use Medicare Part B and Tricare. "It will still cost me 420 a month."

Others said FEHB still compares favorably with what they could buy elsewhere.

One user said, "Self plus one for us in the 400s a month is impossible to beat," adding that private insurance would cost "many, many times that."

More background

Retirees are also weighing provider networks, deductibles, Medicare coordination, and the income-based surcharge known as IRMAA, which can raise Medicare Part B costs for higher earners.

For some, avoiding IRMAA is a major reason to keep FEHB.

One user called that "a very underrated benefit" and said that, once pensions, investment income, and IRA withdrawals are counted, their Part B premiums could be "something like $1,100/month."

Another user said, "This is the way, and no IRMAA."

Serious health scares also shaped the conversation.

One retiree said, "My husband almost died 2 years ago with extended hospitalization and rehab. We have standard BCBS and Medicare B. We paid nothing."

What can be done?

A lower-cost option mentioned in the thread was changing enrollment type.

One user advised, "If you don't have young children, you can move down to self or self+1." That shift alone can lower premiums compared with family coverage.

Users appeared more inclined to switch plans within FEHB than leave the system entirely.

The OP said, "Probably going to BCBS Focus or GEHA Standard is the safer play. It's less than half the cost of BCBS Standard."

Another retiree said they were leaving MHBP for GEHA because MHBP premiums looked too steep.

The ACA option came up mainly as a strategy for retirees who can tightly control taxable income. The OP said that premiums "can end up $0 on ACA" if adjusted gross income stays low enough for subsidies, but warned that "the plan may be crap with a narrow network and high deductibles, so really varies a lot by state."

Travel concerns surfaced too. One user warned that Medicare Advantage FEHB options may not pay for care on cruises because ships are treated as foreign.

They added, "If you go with a MA plan and cruise or travel internationally, consider travel insurance."

Where can I learn more?

Federal retirees aren't the only ones feeling squeezed by insurance costs. These stories look at rising home insurance premiums and climate-driven insurer losses.

• In Oklahoma, homeowners are paying 194% more for coverage than the national average.

• State Farm sought a 30% rate increase, intensifying pressure on already strained homeowners.

• Insurers are absorbing skyrocketing climate-related losses, a trend keeping premiums elevated.

title: DRIVE Act Would Help Veterans Afford the Trip to Care - MOAA
description:
For veterans who travel long distances for medical appointments, access to earned care starts well before they reach the clinic.
Yet VA’s mileage reimbursement rate has remained stuck at 41.5 cents per mile since 2008.
Veterans must cover today’s transportation costs with a reimbursement rate built for a different economy.
For an eligible 100-mile round trip, the difference between the GSA rate and the VA rate is $34.50 before any applicable VA deductible.
Veterans’ earned health care should remain within reach, including the miles between home and the appointment.
text:
For veterans who travel long distances for medical appointments, access to earned care starts well before they reach the clinic. Transportation costs can strain a household budget, especially for veterans on a fixed income or those whose treatment requires repeated visits.

Yet VA’s mileage reimbursement rate has remained stuck at 41.5 cents per mile since 2008. Nearly 18 years without an increase has allowed inflation to steadily erode the benefit’s purchasing power. Veterans must cover today’s transportation costs with a reimbursement rate built for a different economy.

The bipartisan, bicameral Driver Reimbursement Increase for Veteran Equity (DRIVE) Act, led in the House by Rep. Julia Brownley (D-Calif.) and in the Senate by Sen. Peter Welch (D-Vt.), would address that gap.

The legislation would require VA’s mileage reimbursement rate to be at least equal to the General Services Administration (GSA) rate for federal employees using personal vehicles on official business when no government vehicle is available – 76 cents per mile as of July 1, 2026. It also would require mileage reimbursements to be paid within 90 days after a request is properly submitted.

[RELATED: Court Ruling Exposes VA’s Limited Power to Stop Predatory Claims Companies]

The disparity is substantial. For an eligible 100-mile round trip, the difference between the GSA rate and the VA rate is $34.50 before any applicable VA deductible. For veterans making several trips each month, that shortfall adds up quickly.

MOAA Life member H. James Hulton III, a former Air Force captain who served during the Vietnam War era, captured that concern in a recent letter he addressed to the VA secretary: “A reimbursement rate that has not kept pace with fuel and vehicle costs effectively asks veterans to subsidize their own health care travel out of pocket — the opposite of what this benefit was designed to do. For a veteran on a fixed income, the difference between 41.5 cents and 76 cents a mile, multiplied over dozens of appointments a year, is not a rounding error. It is real money that determines whether a veteran can afford to keep the appointment at all.”

[RELATED: Army May Revisit Arlington National Cemetery Eligibility Rule]

Keeping a vehicle ready for regular medical travel carries costs beyond gasoline. A rate that remains unchanged through years of inflation shifts more of that burden onto veterans and their families. The impact can be especially significant for rural veterans and those who need frequent specialty care.

The VA secretary can adjust the mileage rate without new legislation, but the DRIVE Act would establish a stronger standard by linking it to the GSA reimbursement rate, helping the benefit keep pace as that benchmark changes.

Congress and the VA share an opportunity to strengthen access to care by addressing the cost of reaching it. The DRIVE Act offers a bipartisan path toward a more responsive travel benefit and timely payments. Veterans’ earned health care should remain within reach, including the miles between home and the appointment.

text:
As the community settles into fall, the Top of Alabama Regional Council of Gover…

Who is your hero and why?



Fox Army Health Center is increasing warfighter readiness again this quarter through a flu shot campaign that began in late September.

The campaign comes after Secretary of War Pete Hegseth stated that the flu vaccine is optional for the armed forces. The policy has been in place since 1945 and saw another brief rescinding in 1949.

“Our men and women in uniform were forced to choose between their conscience and their country. Even when those decisions posed no threat to our military readiness. You know what I’m talking about, what happened during COVID-19,” Hegseth said during a video statement posted to the social media platform X in April. “No more; that era of betrayal is over. … We’re seizing this moment to discard any absurd, overreaching mandates that only weaken our warfighting capabilities.”

However, a flu outbreak in the Air Force led to their reinstatement of the mandate in July, which subsequently led to the reinstatement of the policy for the Navy and Marines.

For Redstone Arsenal, flu vaccination is mandatory for those assigned to or participating in basic training, forces preparing for deployment, immediate response force service members, first responders, Army personnel working in a medical unit, confinement inmates and staff and Child and Youth Services staff.

“This campaign will be available for all Tricare beneficiaries,” Lt. Col. Aimee Mack, commander of Fox Army Health Center, said.

Mack said appointments can be made and that walk-ins are welcome. Hours for the shots are 8 a.m. to noon and then 1-3 p.m. On Oct. 23, during Retiree Appreciation Day, attendees can expect Fox to be present with the vaccine for their Retiree Appreciation Day flu drive.

She also said that if a team or group of people are looking to get flu shots done simultaneously, they can reach out to the health center. “Scheduling will be done and we’ll send over a team to get your group shots done.”

Mack said Fox accepts outside X-ray orders, also for those with Tricare insurance. However, it is important to note that X-rays are the only radiology service currently available at Fox.

“If you have a written X-ray order, we can complete them here at Fox, our radiology department would be glad to schedule it,” she said.

Those interested in scheduling an appointment can call 256-955-8888. Mack also mentioned that there has been an abundance of no shows, and since the health center is short-staffed, cancellations in advance are encouraged.

text:
Disconnect to farms

The content of Monday's newspaper is rather exemplary of the lack of consistent reporting on agricultural economic issues in Arkansas. Agriculture is seemingly the largest driver of Arkansas' economy. But Monday there was not one significant article about the agricultural businesses.

So when this newspaper wails about declining subscriptions with likely three-fourths of the citizens having some relationship or attachment to the rural farming community, it is not surprising that the print media such as this one fails to thrive.

Could there possibly be an a-ha moment? Take the Democrat-Gazette team on a weekend retreat to a working farm and get some dirt between your fingers and toes so they can understand where agricultural produce and food is manufactured. And then report on it.

THOMAS J. ALSTON

Texarkana

Veterans' medicines

On April 16, 2025, the General Assembly of Arkansas approved, and Gov. Sarah Sanders signed, Act 624, which effectively denies active-duty service members and their families, and retired military personnel including reserve component retirees and their families, the right to use one of the benefits given to us by the U.S. Congress, that of receiving our prescription medications by mail through Express Scripts, the Department of Defense TRICARE selected provider.

The law that was passed requires the state pharmacy board to revoke the license of pharmacies that have Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBM) outside Arkansas. PBMs deal with negotiations and payments throughout the supply chain. This was done, at the request of the pharmacy lobby, to force the above-mentioned personnel to purchase their medications at local pharmacies or obtain them from one of the three VA pharmacies located in Arkansas. All three are in the Little Rock area. The end result will be that in order to use the pharmacy benefit, veterans will have to make long trips. Many are disabled and will have to have someone assist them for the up to 400-mile round trip. It is not likely that the three pharmacies can adequately accommodate the 182,000 veterans who live in Arkansas.

After this law was made public, both Express Scripts and CVS, the other entity affected, filed lawsuits against the state. U.S. District Judge Brian Miller issued a preliminary injunction against the act. The state immediately challenged the ruling. The case continues in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Arkansas. A recent check of their website shows that it is still an active case.

Upon realizing the implications of this act, I contacted Governor Sanders' office, hoping that she would come to the aid of the veterans of Arkansas. No acknowledgment, no response. I further contacted the office of Sen. Tom Cotton, a fellow veteran, asking for his assistance. No acknowledgment, no response.

The midterm elections are coming soon. Guess for whom I will not vote.

HAROLD JOHNSON

Arkadelphia

Artificial intelligence

Surely I am not the first person to predict a war between AI companies. Is competitive nature inherent in AI? What would happen in such a war?

CHARLIE BISHOP

Mabelvale

Mocking of humans

As a 69-year-old resident of Hot Springs Village, I recently registered as an unaffiliated voter in Arkansas. For nearly 45 years, I was a registered Republican and conservative voter; I couldn't count on one hand the number of Democratic candidates I've ever voted for.

Recently, however, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders has pushed me even further away from the Republican Party through her recent political advertisements concerning welfare and transgender policy initiatives.

To be clear, I am not opposed to reasonable work requirements for able-bodied welfare recipients, nor am I opposed to athletics department policies restricting biological males from participating in girls' sports. What I strongly oppose is the governor's decision to air ads that actively mock human beings--those who are less fortunate than her, and those who are struggling to find their way in this world with sexual identity issues.

Governor Sanders, I assume, considers herself a faithful evangelical Christian committed to spreading the Gospel. Yet Jesus plainly taught in the Sermon on the Mount: "Judge not, that ye be not judged." The governor's advertisements run completely contrary to her profession of faith and represent an endorsement of the ugly, divisive politics currently cursing our culture.

These ads are not "Making America Great Again"--they are simply making us look cruel and unkind. I hope the governor reads this letter and helps me understand: How can she reconcile these advertisements with a life lived as a follower of Christ?

BOB GREGG

Hot Springs Village

text:

Kevin D. Curry, 64, of Frisco, Texas, was convicted by a federal jury on September 24 after prosecutors accused him of running a sprawling healthcare fraud, kickback and money-laundering scheme through three mental health clinics in Texas and Florida. The Justice Department announced the conviction on September 25.

Between September 2022 and December 2025, Curry operated Acuity TMS clinics in Plano and Fort Worth, Texas, and Emerald Coast TMS in Fort Walton Beach, Florida. The locations were close to major military communities, including Eglin Air Force Base, Hurlburt Field and Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth.

The clinics billed TRICARE more than $26 million for transcranial magnetic stimulation, or TMS, therapy. According to prosecutors, some treatments were medically unnecessary, some were never provided and others involved patients who did not qualify.

TRICARE ultimately paid about $17 million.

Prosecutors said Curry went even further. He allegedly offered and paid more than $5.5 million in illegal kickbacks to persuade active-duty service members, veterans and their family members to agree to treatments. Employees were also directed to fabricate medical records, while Curry allegedly used doctors’ credentials without their knowledge to support fraudulent claims.

Then came the spending.

Federal prosecutors said Curry used some of the money for luxury hotel stays, a lavish casino-themed party and a gold-plated Tesla Cybertruck valued at more than $100,000. Federal authorities seized the Cybertruck in January along with other assets connected to the case.

The case became a joint investigation involving the Defense Criminal Investigative Service, FBI, Texas Medicaid Fraud Control Unit and the Department of Veterans Affairs Office of Inspector General.

The jury ultimately convicted Curry on three counts of healthcare fraud, three counts involving illegal healthcare kickbacks and three counts involving transactions with criminally derived property.

He has not yet been sentenced.

Curry faces a maximum of 10 years in federal prison on each of the nine counts, although his eventual sentence will be determined by a federal judge under federal sentencing rules.

The strange image of a gold Cybertruck may be what makes the case go viral. But behind it is a much more serious question: how did millions of dollars intended for the healthcare of America's military community end up financing luxury spending?

For the troops, veterans and families whose care was allegedly used to generate the money, the gold truck is more than an outrageous purchase. It is the most visible symbol of where the prosecutors say the money went.

Editor’s Note: Curry was convicted by a federal jury and is presumed innocent of any charges for which he was not convicted. The allegations described above are based on evidence presented at trial and statements from the U.S. Department of Justice. Curry is scheduled to be sentenced at a later date.

text:
Genito-urological Injuries Increased in Warfighters After 2001

WASHINGTON — Nearly 2,000 U.S. troops suffered debilitating injuries to their groins or genitals during the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan between 2000 and 2013, and about 307,000 more sustained some type of head injury over the same period, all injuries that can compromise fertility and sexual function. Those figures illustrate the stakes behind family-planning decisions made ahead of a combat deployment and motivate a new Pentagon program that will help troops preserve before they deploy their ability to have children.

A notice published in the Federal Register on Aug. 13 announced that the DoD will launch a 3-year demonstration project on Sept. 14 that reimburses eligible active-duty servicemembers for the cost of freezing sperm or eggs. The benefit will cover up to $500 a year in sperm cryopreservation costs. The reimbursement rises to $10,000 a year for egg, or oocyte, cryopreservation, reflecting the far higher cost and complexity of egg retrieval, which typically requires hormone stimulation and a surgical procedure, compared with sperm banking.

The program, required by Section 709 of the Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025, is open to active-duty members of the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force and Space Force who meet at least one of three conditions. These include receiving orders for an assignment that qualifies for hazardous duty pay, being likely to receive such orders within 120 days or being separated from a spouse, domestic partner or dating partner for 180 days or more under orders, including sea duty.

Participation is voluntary. Eligible troops can obtain preservation services either at a military treatment facility with a reproductive medicine program or through a civilian clinic of their choosing. Reimbursable costs include gamete retrieval procedures and the medications and lab testing associated with them, cryopreservation itself and the shipping and storage of the samples for the duration of the 3-year demonstration.

Because the Defense Health Agency does not have visibility into deployment orders, commanders must validate a servicemember’s eligibility before reimbursement is approved. Troops must submit a complete DHA Form 459, along with itemized invoices, within 120 days of the date services began, typically the date of retrieval or the associated lab procedure or prescription. Servicemembers could be eligible for reimbursement more than once during the 3-year pilot, if they again meet the eligibility criteria.

Participants also will be required to attest that they have an advance medical directive specifying what should happen to their preserved gametes in the event of their death. Decisions about continued storage, disposition or future use after the demonstration period remain solely the responsibility of the servicemember and fall outside the scope of the program, according to the notice.

The program has been more than a decade in coming. In 2016, then-Defense Secretary Ash Carter announced a similar pilot as part of a broader package of family-friendly policies, saying the department wanted to help troops preserve their ability to start a family even after a combat injury. That earlier program never got off the ground. This time, the effort comes with a congressional mandate and a defined evaluation plan: The Pentagon will track how many servicemembers use the benefit, its total cost, the administrative burden of running it and its effects on force readiness, retention and member satisfaction during the pilot period.

Military families and support organizations have pushed for such benefits for years. Improvised explosive devices (IEDs) were the signature weapon of the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, causing thousands of severe combat casualties and complex, multi-system trauma. Among the most devastating were urotrauma and pelvic injuries. Severe blast winds and ground-strike detonations caused devastating damage to the pelvis, urinary tract, and reproductive organs.

In a 2023 study, a Rutgers University research team used predefined search criteria to primarily identify any casualties that arrived at a military treatment facility with urological-based injuries. The found that the registry contained 25,897 adult casualties, of which 7.2% sustained urological injuries.1

The median age for injury was 25, and explosive injuries (64%) and firearms (27%) were the primary causes. Most patients survived until hospital discharge (94%). The authors pointed out that the most frequently injured organs were the scrotum (60%), testes (53%), penis (30%), and kidneys (30%).

“The incidence of genitourinary trauma persistently increased for both military and civilian personnel as the U.S. remained actively engaged in major military conflicts during this period,” the study concluded. “Patients with genitourinary trauma in this data set were often associated with high injury severity scores and required an increased number of immediate and long-term resources for survival and rehabilitation.”

The injuries weren’t just immediate and physical, however. In 2014, the Bob Woodruff Foundation convened a conference examining how combat injuries affect intimacy and family planning, and many nonprofits have offered free or discounted cryopreservation services to some servicemembers in the interim. Until now, however, deploying servicemembers who wanted to bank sperm or eggs as a hedge against combat injury or prolonged separation have had to pay for it themselves, and some military families have described going to considerable lengths, including seeking emergency cryopreservation after a servicemember was critically injured, to maintain their options to have children.

Whether the new benefit becomes permanent will likely hinge on how the demonstration project affects retention. Beyond tracking cost and participation, the Pentagon has said it wants to understand whether offering the benefit affects how troops and their families view deployments and long separations, a question that goes to the heart of recruitment and retention pressures the services have faced in recent years. For now, the reimbursement applies only for the length of the three-year pilot, though the notice leaves open the possibility that the department could extend it through a subsequent Federal Register notice.

description:

AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) provides care and services to HIV patients in the United States and other countries.

text:
AIDS Healthcare Foundation, a non-profit organization based in Los Angeles, California, has agreed to pay $1.44 million to resolve allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by submitting or failing to delete false or invalid diagnosis codes in order to increase payments that it received from the Medicare Advantage program. “The government relies on Medicare Advantage participants to submit accurate, substantiated diagnosis codes that are adequately documented in a medical record to ensure proper payment,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.

Key details of the case

“The Justice Department will continue to protect the public fisc and hold accountable those who receive inflated payments by knowingly providing or failing to correct false information.”. “The integrity of our federal healthcare programs, including Medicare Advantage, must be preserved,” said First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California.

Moreover, “We will not tolerate companies undermining the interests of Medicare patients for financial gain.”. “Medicare Advantage organizations have a responsibility to ensure the accuracy of diagnosis codes they submit for payment. When entities fail to correct information they know is wrong, they undermine the integrity of a program millions of seniors rely on,” said Acting Deputy Inspector General for Investigations Miranda L.

Bennett of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS‑OIG). “HHS‑OIG will continue to safeguard taxpayer funds by holding organizations accountable when their failures inflate federal payments and compromise program trust.”.

Enforcement actions and official statements

In addition, under the Medicare Advantage (MA) Program, also known as Medicare Part C, Medicare beneficiaries may opt out of traditional Medicare and enroll in private health plans offered by insurance companies known as Medicare Advantage Organizations. MAOs. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) pays the MAOs a fixed monthly amount for each Medicare beneficiary enrolled in their plans.

CMS adjusts these monthly payments to account for various “risk” factors that affect expected health expenditures for the beneficiary. In general, CMS pays MAOs more for sicker beneficiaries expected to incur higher healthcare costs and less for healthier beneficiaries expected to incur lower costs. To calculate the payment amounts, CMS uses a health-based risk adjustment model. For complete details, refer to the official DOJ press release.

Consequently, the Hierarchical Conditions Category (HCC) model — that takes into account diagnoses reported by healthcare providers. In general, the more severe the diagnosis or costly the associated treatment, the higher the risk score and the higher the corresponding payments to the MAO. Diagnosis codes submitted to CMS must be supported by the beneficiaries’ medical records and be accurate, complete.

Truthful, based on the best knowledge, information, and belief of the MAO making the submission. AIDS Healthcare Foundation (AHF) provides care and services to HIV patients in the United States and other countries. AHF’s Managed Care Division (doing business as Positive Healthcare Partners) operated special needs MA plans for Medicare beneficiaries who have HIV and lived in Florida, Georgia. For related coverage, see Kevin Curry convicted in $26 million TRICARE fraud and kickback scheme.

California. The settlement announced today resolves allegations that, for payment years 2017 to 2023, AHF failed to timely investigate and delete diagnosis codes that were either inaccurate or not documented in medical records. Beginning in around 2017, AHF’s risk adjustment coders conducted chart reviews to identify inaccurate or unsupported diagnosis codes for deletion.

As part of this process, AHF’s risk adjustment coders maintained “Delete Research” spreadsheets. Listed diagnosis codes they identified as potentially lacking support in the medical record but needing further research. Although AHF knew that it was required to investigate and delete inaccurate and unsupported diagnosis codes within 60 days, AHF failed to timely investigate and delete the codes. For related coverage, see Independence Blue Cross (IBX) to Pay $22.5 Million to Resolve False Claims Act Allegations.

At the same time, aHF did not delete most of the inaccurate or unsupported diagnosis codes in the “Delete Research” spreadsheets until 2024 or 2025. Well after AHF was on notice that the codes potentially lacked support and only after being notified of the United States’ investigation. The United States further alleges that, for payment year 2017, AHF knowingly submitted diagnosis codes for HIV (ICD-10 B20) where the diagnosis was not documented in any medical record for a face-to-face visit, in violation of CMS requirements that all diagnosis code submissions must be documented as a result of a face-to-face visit.

In particular, the civil settlement resolves claims brought under the qui tam or whistleblower provisions of the False Claims Act by Donna Irons, a former risk adjustment coder at AHF. Under the qui tam provisions, a private party can file an action on behalf of the United States and receive a portion of any recovery. The qui tam case is captioned United States ex rel.

Furthermore, aIDS Healthcare Foundation d/b/a Positive Healthcare Partners, Civil Action No. 23-cv-2160 (C.D. Irons will receive $259,200 as her share of the federal recovery. AHF received credit under the Department of Justice’s guidelines for taking disclosure, cooperation.

Investigation and prosecution details

Remediation into account in False Claims Act resolutions, Justice Manual § 4-4.112. In addition to cooperating in the government’s investigation and enhancing its compliance program, AHF proactively remediated its conduct during the course of Department’s investigation by submitting deletes for diagnosis codes that, based on review of medical records, were not supported. The resolution obtained in this matter was the result of a coordinated effort between the Justice Department’s Civil Division, Commercial Litigation Branch, Fraud Section and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Central District of California, with assistance from the Department of Health and Human Services, Office of Inspector General.
